ety.text: Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō)bor. Latin gubernāre Old French governer Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -ment Old French governementbor. Middle English governement English government From Middle English governement, from Old French governement (modern French gouvernement), from governer (see govern) + -ment. Morphologically govern + -ment. Displaced native Old English gerec, leodweard, ræden, rǣding and ealdordōm.

senses.d: The body with the power to make and/or enforce laws to control a country, land area, people or organization.
ex: British government has historically centred exclusively on London.
[…]and that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.

senses.d: The relationship between a word and its dependents.
The state and its administration viewed as the ruling political power.
ex: Near-synonyms: state, administration
If the citizens must follow the law, then the government must follow the constitution.

senses.d: The management or control of a system.
ex: The government of the Church is maintained without material alteration in a settled hierarchical form.

senses.d: The tenure of a head of government; the ministry or administration led by a specified individual.
ex: The Sunak government announced plans to stem the flow of migrants coming into Great Britain.

senses.d: In a parliamentary system, the political party or coalition in power; its condition of being in power.
The team tasked with presenting and speaking in favour of a resolution, as opposed to the opposition.
A guberniya.
ex: with its centre in Liubawitz, in the Government of Mohilev.

grp.label: body with the power to make and/or enforce laws

Middle English governour English governor From Middle English governour, from Old French gouvreneur, from Latin gubernator, from Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman, pilot, guide”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, to drive, to guide, to act as a pilot”), of disputed origin. By surface analysis, govern + -or. Doublet of gubernator.

senses.d: The chief executive officer of a first-level administrative division of a country.
ex: Younger voters are more libertarian in political philosophy than older voters and are credited with the success of libertarian governor Jesse Ventura of Minnesota.
But gender is a factor both candidates will navigate in a country that has elected just 51 female state governors in its history.

senses.d: A device which regulates or controls some action of a machine through automatic feedback.
ex: A governor on the injection pump limits the speed when running idle.

senses.d: A member of a decision-making body (such as a committee) for a larger organization or entity (including some public agencies), similar to or equivalent to a board of directors (used especially for banks); a member of the board of governors.
ex: The seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

senses.d: Term of address to a man.
ex: "Oh, right you are, governor, if you say so," accepted Fank […]

senses.d: A superior, especially a boss, an employer, or (law enforcement) a superior police officer.
Synonym of father.
A constituent of a phrase that governs another.
One who has the care or guardianship of a young man; a tutor; a guardian.
A pilot; a steersman.

From Middle English governen, governe, from Anglo-Norman and Old French governer, guverner, from Latin gubernō, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, govern”). Displaced native Old English wealdan, whence modern dialectical English wald (“to govern”).

senses.d: To make and administer the public policy and affairs of; to exercise sovereign authority in.
ex: The old king governed the land wisely.

senses.d: To exercise political authority; to run a government.
To control the actions or behavior of; to keep under control; to restrain.
ex: Govern yourselves like civilized people.
a student who could not govern his impulses

senses.d: To exercise a deciding or determining influence on.
ex: Chance governs the outcome of many card games.

senses.d: To have or exercise a determining influence.
To handle, to manage, to oversee (a matter, an affair, a household, etc.).
To control the speed, flow etc. of; to regulate.
ex: a valve that governs fuel intake

senses.d: To direct the course of, to guide in some direction, to steer.
To look after, to take care of, to tend to (someone or some plant).
ex:
from my vncles country of Medea,
Where all my youth I haue bene gouerned, […]

senses.d: To manage, to control, to work (a tool or mechanical device).
